properties.name: Paul Gauguin
properties.biography: A sailor, stockbroker, art collector, dealer, and father of five children with his Danish wife, Gauguin found himself destitute after the stock market crash of 1882. Separated from his family, he became an artist with the encouragement of Camille Pissarro and Claude Emile Schuffenecker. Stints in Brittany and Provence (visiting Vincent van Gogh in 1888) remained transitory, and Gauguin left Europe in 1891 for French Polynesia. With the exception of a return visit to Paris in 1893–95, he remained there for the rest of his life.

properties.name: John Ruskin
properties.biography: As a child, Ruskin was an enthusiastic student of literature, art, and geology, interests that would sustain him throughout his life. He studied art with James Duffield Harding, among others, and became a skilled amateur artist, creating sensitive drawings and watercolors of landscapes and architecture. Ruskin is best known for his voluminous and highly influential writings about art, including Modern Painters (1843–60) and The Stones of Venice (1851–53). He was a collector and rigorous champion of works by J. M. W. Turner.

properties.name: Georges Michel
properties.biography: Despite his modest family background, Michel trained with an academic painter, exhibited in the Salon between 1791 and 1814, and even found employment as a restorer of Dutch landscape paintings by Rembrandt, Jacob van Ruisdael, and Meindert Hobbema at the Louvre. He drew and painted Montmartre and the plain of St. Denis throughout his life, which earned him loyal support from Baron d’Ivry, his main benefactor. Michel was admired by the Barbizon artists and Vincent van Gogh.

properties.name: Claude-Louis Chatelet
properties.biography: As a topographical artist and illustrator, Châtelet depicted parks in the vicinity of Paris and traveled on assignment. He repeatedly visited Switzerland and spent time in southern Italy recording landscapes for the Abbé de Saint-Non’s travel descriptions, published between 1781 and 1786. During the French Revolution, Châtelet was a Jacobin and died on the guillotine.

properties.name: Thomas Girtin
properties.biography: Girtin was apprenticed to topographical watercolorist Edward Dayes and later joined the informal academy directed by Thomas Monro. Monro assigned fledgling artists Girtin and J. M. W. Turner to copy the drawings by John Robert Cozens in his collection; Girtin was said to have set the outlines while Turner added the wash. Girtin traveled widely in England and visited Paris. During his short life, he developed a style of watercolor characterized by broad swaths of muted color, inspiring a generation of artists such as Richard Parkes Bonington, John Sell Cotman, and John Varley.

properties.name: Joseph Mallord William Turner
properties.biography: Encouraged in his artistic pursuits from a young age, Turner enrolled at London’s Royal Academy at fourteen, studying perspective and watercolor (1789–93). He bolstered his education with many sketching trips and worked side by side with Thomas Girtin under the tutelage of physician and art aficionado Thomas Monro. Made an associate member of the Royal Academy in 1799 and full member in 1802, Turner quickly garnered the attention of critics and wealthy patrons. Travel to France and Switzerland (1802); to Belgium, Holland, and along the Rhine (1817); and to Italy (1819– 20) fed his ambitions as a landscape artist. Many more trips to the continent and throughout Britain followed. His sketches in graphite and watercolor provided inspiration for many paintings that were increasingly dissolved into light-filled swaths of color. Toward the end of his life, he retreated into privacy, misunderstood even by admirers like art critic John Ruskin.

properties.name: Johann Georg von Dillis
properties.biography: An advisor to the Bavarian kings, Dillis helped shape the Alte Pinakothek in Munich through decades of work with royal painting collections (starting in 1790). He was also a prolific artist. His numerous drawings and oil sketches based on regular walks in the vicinity of Munich and travel throughout Europe served as material for classical landscapes in oil on canvas. He taught landscape painting at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts from 1808 to 1814.

properties.name: Christoffer Wilhelm Eckersberg
properties.biography: A stipend from the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts in Copenhagen and support from a benefactor enabled Eckersberg to complete his education in Paris (1810– 13), as a student of Jacques-Louis David, and in Rome (1813–16). Upon his return to Copenhagen, he became a highly influential academic teacher who shaped a generation of Danish artists with his emphasis on figure studies, perspective, and drawing outdoors.

properties.name: Hendrik Voogd
properties.biography: Trained as a landscape painter in Amsterdam, Voogd traveled to Rome for further instruction. He continued to specialize in landscapes, citing Claude Lorrain as his model. An early practitioner of lithography, he produced prints of famous views for tourists and executed many wash drawings of Rome and the campagna. He remained in Italy until his death.

properties.name: James Duffield Harding
properties.biography: Harding specialized in landscapes executed in watercolor and was an early practitioner of lithography, which he used to reproduce his drawings. He published a number of influential drawing manuals as well as compilations of lithographs on tinted paper, including Sketches at Home and Abroad (1836) and Picturesque Selections (1861). Harding was known as an inspiring teacher. John Ruskin, one of his most ardent pupils, called him “unquestionably the greatest master of foliage in Europe.”

properties.name: François-Edouard Bertin
properties.biography: Born into a publishing family, Bertin studied at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris and enjoyed a successful career as a painter. In his works, which he frequently exhibited at the Salon, he drew from his travel experiences in Italy, Greece, the Levant, and Egypt. In 1854, Bertin took over the Journal des débats, a newspaper founded by his father.

properties.name: Théodore Rousseau
properties.biography: Rousseau favored landscape painting from an early age and rejected, during his studies with Guillaume Lethière and others, demands to elevate the observed scenery with classical motifs. He worked in the Forest of Fontainebleau after 1827–28, effectively establishing himself as a leader of the Barbizon School. His work was scorned by the establishment until around 1848, when he became recognized as one of France’s most original landscape painters. Preparatory drawings continued to accompany his painting practice throughout his life.

properties.name: Johan Barthold Jongkind
properties.biography: After initial academic training in The Hague, Jongkind studied with Eugène Isabey in Paris and lived variously in France and the Netherlands throughout his life, specializing in paintings and watercolors of harbors, canals, and Parisian city views. A contributor to the first Salon du Refusés in 1863, he got to know fellow participant Claude Monet, who eagerly learned from Jongkind about atmospheric light effects in outdoor painting.

properties.name: Camille Pissarro
properties.birthplace: St. Thomas, Danish W. Indies (now U.S. Virgin Islands)
properties.biography: Raised in a Sephardic Jewish family from France on the island of St. Thomas, Pissarro attended school in Paris from 1842 to 1847. He established a studio with Danish artist Fritz Melbye in Caracas, Venezuela (1852– 54), before returning to France in 1855. There, he took classes at the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Suisse and copied at the Louvre. A frequent exhibitor at the Salon in the 1860s, he worked side by side with Paul Cézanne and became central to the Impressionist group and their exhibitions in the 1870s and 1880s. He continuously practiced drawing to prepare figurative paintings and created numerous watercolors of the landscape, especially from 1885 to 1890.
properties.biography_life: St. Thomas, Danish W. Indies [now U.S. Virgin Islands] 1830–1903 Paris

properties.name: Félix Henri Bracquemond
properties.biography: As an independently minded printmaker with a great aptitude for reproducing Old Master paintings and for creating highly original portraits, landscapes, and animal studies of his own, Bracquemond garnered accolades for submissions to prestigious exhibitions, such as the Salon and the 1900 Exposition Universelle. He founded the Société des Aquafortistes in 1862; participated in Impressionist exhibitions in 1874, 1879, and 1880; and founded the Société des PeintresGraveurs Français in 1890.

properties.name: Jean-Thomas Thibault
properties.biography: After studying architecture with Étienne-Louis Boullée at the École des Beaux-Arts in Paris (1780–86), Thibault spent four years in Rome in the circle of Charles Percier and Pierre-François-Léonard Fontaine and earned a reputation for his architectural drawings. During the Napoleonic era, he participated in the modernization of the Élysée and Neuilly palaces and converted the Amsterdam town hall into a royal palace for King Louis Bonaparte.

properties.name: Jean-Baptiste-Camille Corot
properties.biography: A student of classical landscape painter Jean-Victor Bertin, Corot traveled to Italy in 1825–28. There, he befriended Claude-Félix-Théodore Caruelle d’Aligny, with whom he explored the countryside on sketching trips. He continued this practice throughout his life, traveling throughout France, Switzerland, Italy, and the Netherlands. By the 1850s, he was one of France’s most influential and collectable painters, a friend of Gustave 285 Artist Biographies Artist Biographies Courbet and admired by Camille Pissarro, Claude Monet, and Berthe Morisot, his student.

properties.name: Claude-Félix-Théodore Caruelle d' Aligny
properties.biography: While in Rome in 1822–27, d’Aligny befriended François-Edouard Bertin and Camille Corot, with whom he explored the countryside on sketching trips. Active in the Forest of Fontainebleau after 1827, d’Aligny submitted landscape paintings to the Paris Salon from 1837 to 1842. During the last decade of his life, he was director of the École des Beaux-Arts in Lyon.

properties.name: Ferdinand-Victor-Eugène Delacroix
properties.biography: Influenced by Théodore Géricault, Delacroix created monumental paintings inspired by literature and contemporary history that soon earned him public attention. Following the 1830 revolution in France, he exhibited his iconic Liberty Leading the People in the Salon of 1831. It was subsequently acquired by the state. A fruitful visit to Morocco in 1832, documented in drawings and watercolors, provided inspiration for decades to come. While he took on large-scale decorative paintings, Delacroix continued to draw and to respond to nature in intimate paintings and watercolors.

properties.name: Paul Cézanne
properties.biography: Independently wealthy for much of his adult life, Cézanne charted his artistic path in conversation with, yet at a critical distance from, Parisian art circles. Through Camille Pissarro, he participated in several exhibitions of Impressionist art, but critics singled him out for ridicule. Searching for compositional solidity in paintings that embraced the atmospheric changes of a world in constant flux, Cézanne found encouragement in the canonical art of the Louvre and the immovable grandeur of local scenery. Mont Sainte-Victoire, near his hometown, became a recurring motif in the last two decades of his life.

properties.name: Caspar Wolf
properties.biography: Wolf had finally settled in Bern, after extensive studies and travel in southern Germany and France, when local publisher Abraham Wagner commissioned two hundred Alpine landscape paintings from him. Based on regular tours into the mountains (1774–78), they were exhibited in Wagner’s gallery along with print reproductions for sale. Wolf exhibited the paintings again in Paris in 1780 and had them reproduced by Jean François Janinet. He organized another exhibition of Alpine scenes at the Palatine Gallery in Düsseldorf.

properties.name: Jean-Antoine Linck
properties.biography: The success of exhibitions of his gouaches in Geneva in 1789 and the following decades enabled Linck to dedicate himself to landscape painting full-time, with clients including empresses Joséphine Bonaparte and Catherine II of Russia. His sought-after mountain views combined geological accuracy and monumentality to great effect.

properties.name: Johann Jakob Meyer
properties.biography: After apprenticing with painter Johann Heinrich Füssli (known as Henry Fuseli) in Zurich, Meyer garnered a reputation for topographical Alpine views in paintings and prints. He frequently left his family in Zurich to draw in the mountains and to travel 292 Artist Biographies throughout Europe in an effort to sell his work, meeting royalty in Berlin and St. Petersburg. In Meyer’s absence, his son Jacques sold his father’s paintings and other belongings and immigrated to the United States. The father died impoverished.

properties.name: Johann Rudolf Koller
properties.biography: A widely traveled painter of landscapes and animals, Koller drew from his studies and travels in Zurich, Düsseldorf, Paris, Munich, and Italy. Honored with medals in Switzerland and abroad, Koller’s wellcomposed Realist paintings dignify the natural environment and idealize country life.

properties.name: Adrian Zingg
properties.biography: After training in Zurich and Bern, Zingg went in 1759 to Paris, where he worked for printer and publisher Johann Georg Wille. In 1764, he took a position at the art academy in Dresden, advancing in 1803 to professor of engraving. His sepia drawings of the vicinity of Dresden were widely admired.

properties.name: Johann Christian Klengel
properties.biography: A visit to Rome in 1790–92 was a revelation for Klengel, who had been trained in Dresden as a landscape painter. Steeped in the tradition of Dutch painters of the seventeenth century, Klengel had been a member of the Dresden Academy since 1777, where he was influenced by Swiss artist Adrian Zingg. He became a professor of landscape painting in Dresden in 1800.

properties.name: Franz Theobald Horny
properties.biography: From a young age, Horny trained with his father, a drawing teacher in Weimar, and, funded by a stipend, with Joseph Anton Koch in Rome after 1816. There, he associated with a German group of expatriates, the Lukasbrüder, but shortly after his return to Germany, fell sick with tuberculosis. His premature death in Olevano, where he sought to restore his health, cut short one of the most promising artistic trajectories of his generation.

properties.name: Caspar David Friedrich
properties.biography: After studies in Greifswald and Copenhagen (1790–98), Friedrich settled in Dresden, where he was influenced by Adrian Zingg and the local landscape tradition. His spiritual and often nationalistic landscape paintings, based on pencil sketches produced outdoors, were soon acquired by the Prussian king. Hoped-for advancements of his career did not materialize, but later generations revered the artist as the leading German Romanticist.

properties.name: Adrian Ludwig Richter
properties.biography: One of Germany’s most prolific illustrators, Richter was best known to his contemporaries for his woodcuts of fairy tales and popular, sentimental literature. His initial training was as a landscapist influenced by Adrian Zingg and, after traveling to Italy, by Joseph Anton Koch and Julius Schnorr von Carolsfeld. Richter was appointed professor of landscape painting at the Dresden Academy in 1836 and continued to produce landscapes in paintings, drawings, and prints.

properties.name: Albertus Brondgeest
properties.biography: Brondgeest was a successful art dealer, copyist of seventeenth-century Dutch paintings, and painter and draftsman of the Dutch landscape. An active participant in Amsterdam art circles, he was a member of the Royal Netherlandish Institute and the Royal Academies of Amsterdam and Antwerp.

properties.name: Adolph Menzel
properties.biography: Menzel, who spent most of his life in Berlin, was a prominent painter, draftsman, and illustrator. He was renowned for his works in all media celebrating the life of the eighteenth-century Prussian monarch Frederick the Great. He was also interested in industrial scenes and church interiors. He drew constantly, using a carpenter’s pencil, and had a coat specially made with multiple pockets to hold his sketchbooks and drawing implements. Menzel’s works are characterized by a high degree of observation and realism.

properties.name: Lovis Corinth
properties.biography: Born into a farming family, Corinth studied in academies in Königsberg and Munich and at the Académie Julian in Paris between 1876 and 1887. He moved to Berlin in 1902, exhibited with the Berlin Secession group (and became its president in 1915), and was championed by art dealer Paul Cassirer.
properties.biography_life: Tapiau, East Prussia [now Gvardeysk, Russia] 1858– 1925 Zandvoort, Netherlands

properties.name: Paul Sandby
properties.biography: Trained as a military draftsman, Sandby was well attuned to the demands of topographical drawing, which informed his work throughout his life. He specialized in landscape views, mostly watercolors and etchings, finding particular inspiration in the vicinity of Windsor Castle. He published two series of prints of prospects in Wales, taking advantage of aquatint, a recently invented printing technique, to simulate wash drawings. Sandby was a founding member of London’s Royal Academy, established in 1768, and exhibited his works there annually. He was also an influential drawing master.

properties.name: John Constable
properties.biography: Constable was trained at the Royal Academy Schools, London, but decided against a career as an academic drawing teacher. Instead, he dedicated himself to the depiction of Suffolk County, where he was raised. Constable imbued landscape painting with both optical accuracy and emotional connection. His increasingly ambitious paintings, scaled to impress audiences in public exhibitions, were based on incessant drawing. When two of his paintings were shown at the Paris Salon in 1824, they received enthusiastic praise and inspired artists such as Eugène Delacroix.

properties.name: John Varley
properties.biography: A cofounder of the Society of Painters in WaterColours, John Varley exhibited there regularly and was a leading proponent of watercolor’s luminous properties. He is best known for his topographical views of towns in England and Wales, as well as his landscapes. He was a popular teacher, counting both professional artists and amateurs among his pupils and recommending that they draw directly from nature. His influential volume Treatise on the Principles of Landscape Design was published in 1816–17.

properties.name: Cornelius Varley
properties.biography: Like his elder brother, John, Cornelius Varley was a landscape painter who was part of the artist group 296 around Thomas Monro. Although he was one of the founders of the Society of Painters in Water-Colours, he rarely exhibited his works, which at the time were dismissed as pedestrian. Cornelius invented optical instruments such as the graphic telescope and other tools that allowed artists to project images onto paper. He also cofounded the Royal Microscopical Society.

properties.name: David Cox
properties.biography: When he arrived in London in 1804, Cox sought lessons from John Varley, soon exhibited with the Royal Academy, and took on leadership roles in associations for watercolorists, especially the Society of Painters in Water-Colours (from 1812). He became a dedicated teacher himself and published several highly regarded treatises on watercolor practice. Between 1844 and 1856, he visited North Wales yearly, and the region became a dominant theme in his work, increasingly characterized by his use of coarse Scottish wrapping paper as a support and loose, broad strokes.

properties.name: Ellis Cornelia Knight
properties.biography: Knight’s posthumously published memoirs trace her upbringing in London, as the highly educated daughter of an admiral, and her life in Rome and Naples with her mother, in the circle of Sir William and Lady Hamilton. In Italy, she found time to create watercolors of picturesque sites. She returned to England in 1799 with Lady Hamilton, in the company of Lord Nelson. Knight was appointed companion to Queen Charlotte in 1805 and to Princess Charlotte in 1813–14. She traveled throughout Europe as a socialite for the last two decades of her life.

properties.name: Théodore Géricault
properties.biography: After initial training in Parisian painters’ ateliers, Géricault copied works from the European tradition at the Louvre (1811–15) and went to Rome, where he was overwhelmed by the city’s art historical legacy as well as contemporary life. After his masterpiece The Raft of the Medusa received mixed reviews at the Paris Salon, 288 Artist Biographies Géricault spent time in London, enamored by the local equestrian culture and its imagery.

properties.name: Jean-François Millet
properties.biography: Millet moved from Paris to the village of Barbizon, near the Forest of Fontainebleau, in 1849 and remained there for the rest of his life. Working alongside artists such as Théodore Rousseau and Narcisse Virgile Diaz de la Peña, he became known as one of the Barbizon School. The Barbizon artists eschewed the classical landscape tradition, favoring the humble subjects popularized by seventeenth-century Dutch painters. Millet’s paintings and pastels featured rural figures and their environs; in famous works such as The Sower (1850) and The Angelus (1857–59), these figures came to be understood as embodying aspects of shared human experience, such as hard work and religious devotion.

properties.name: Vincent van Gogh
properties.biography: Born into a Dutch pastor’s family and trained at art dealerships in The Hague, London, and Paris, Van Gogh was active as a rural missionary before becoming an artist. Tremendously prolific in the last ten years of his life (1880–90) but unable to sustain himself financially, he worked in the Netherlands, Antwerp, and Paris before moving to Arles in southern France. Influenced by Anton Mauve, Jean-François Millet, and Eugène Delacroix, he was introduced to members of the Parisian avant-garde by his brother Theo, an art dealer. Hopes of establishing an artist colony in Arles, in 1888, with Paul Gauguin, ended tragically. After months of hospitalization, Van Gogh returned to Paris and died by suicide.

properties.name: Jozef Israëls
properties.biography: Studies at the Royal Academy of Fine Arts in Amsterdam (1844–50), interrupted by a stay in Paris (1845–47), set Israëls on the path to becoming the most distinguished Dutch painter of his generation. After 1871, he was a leader of the so-called Hague School, whose members are recognized for their realism and commitment to highlighting marginalized communities. Widely exhibited, collected, and reproduced, Israëls maintained many institutional and personal connections abroad. He influenced younger artists, such as Vincent van Gogh.

properties.name: Edouard Manet
properties.biography: After studying with Thomas Couture and gaining practice by copying Italian and Dutch paintings at the Louvre, Manet began to exhibit in 1859, polarizing public opinion with provocative paintings that later became icons of art history. Attuned to modern urban life and open to various sources of inspiration found while traveling and at home in Paris, he was supported by loyal friends, such as poet and critic Charles Baudelaire, and challenged by rivals, including Edgar Degas. Berthe Morisot was his sister-in-law. Manet, who fought the German invasion in the French National Guard in 1870, succumbed to health challenges at age fifty-one.

properties.name: Georges Pierre Seurat
properties.biography: Seurat was the father of pointillism, a practice based on the analytic understanding of color and form and research into human perception. He found encouragement in the work of Italian Renaissance painter Piero della Francesca and sought out Pierre Puvis de Chavannes as a mentor. His first public success came with his participation in the Salon des Indépendants in 1884 and the eighth Impressionist exhibition in 1886. As a member of a small circle of avant-garde artists and intellectuals in Montmartre, he dedicated himself to elaborate figurative compositions, interrupted by summer sketching trips to Normandy and Brittany. His characteristic conte crayon drawings on Michallet paper could be preparatory for his paintings or independent works of art.

properties.name: Hendrik Willem Mesdag
properties.biography: Mesdag was one of the primary members of the Hague School, an informal group of artists who lived and worked in that city, close to the seaside resort of Scheveningen. There, he found his signature subject: atmospheric marine views of sailboats and fishing vessels. He was head of the Pulchri Studio artists’ association and active in the Dutch Drawing Society founded in 1876. A discerning collector, Mesdag owned an important assemblage of contemporary works by Dutch artists and French painters associated with the Barbizon School, now exhibited in a museum called the Mesdag Collection in The Hague.

properties.name: Winslow Homer
properties.biography: Trained as an illustrator, Homer served as a correspondent for Harper’s Weekly during the U.S. Civil War. His early paintings feature that conflagration as well as views of leisurely life on the shore and in the countryside. A sojourn in England and time spent on the coast of Maine led to muscular paintings and watercolors of fisherfolk and the elemental power of the ocean. Homer repaired to a studio in the seaside resort of Prouts Neck, Maine, in 1883 and made several trips to Florida and the Bahamas, producing a surfeit of vibrant watercolors that have influenced artists for generations.

properties.name: John Singer Sargent
properties.biography: Born to American parents in Florence, Sargent spent most of his life in Europe, with occasional trips to the United States. He settled in Paris in 1874, exhibiting his best-known painting, Madame X (Virginie Amélie Avegno Gautreau), in 1884. Shortly thereafter he moved to London, where he became known for his lush society portraits. Sargent was a prodigious and expert watercolorist; many of his works represent his summer sojourns in the Alps. Toward the end of his life, he was preoccupied with mural projects for the Boston Public Library, Widener Library at Harvard, and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston.

properties.name: Johan Hendrik van Mastenbroek
properties.biography: Van Mastenbroek, an alumnus of the Rotterdam Academy, is best known for his impressionistic views of the city’s harbor, one of Europe’s busiest. In 1931, he received a government commission to document the land reclamation at the Zuiderzee, a major engineering project that reshaped the topography of the Netherlands. Rotterdam was nearly completely destroyed in World War II, giving Van Mastenbroek’s paintings and watercolors of the city added meaning as elegiac documents of loss.

properties.name: Jean-Michel Moreau, called Moreau le jeune
Félix Vallotton
properties.biography: As a student at the Académie Julian in Paris, where he enrolled in 1882, Vallotton first excelled in portrait painting, which he presented at the Salon. In 1892, Vallotton joined the Nabis group and exhibited with them frequently, developing an immediately recognizable style of psychologically intense interior scenes, depictions of modern city life, and precisely rendered landscapes. Extremely prolific and versatile, he was active as an illustrator and printmaker and contributed to the international revival of woodcut in the 1890s.

properties.name: William Gilpin
properties.biography: Gilpin was ordained as a clergyman in 1746 and held positions in several parishes. He was also a biographer and an enlightened and influential schoolmaster. He helped refine the definition of the term “picturesque” in a series of essays, or “Observations,” that developed from his travels in Britain. Sketchbook and drawing materials in hand, he sought views that were “agreeable in a picture,” thus adding a third category to the established aesthetic ideals of “the sublime” and “the beautiful.” He published numerous books of aquatint reproductions of his landscape wash drawings.

properties.name: Sir John Frederick William Herschel
properties.biography: Herschel was a Cambridge-trained mathematician, astronomer, and chemist who has been called Britain’s first modern physical scientist. Working closely with William Henry Fox Talbot (1800–1877), he made contributions to the field of photochemistry with significance for the advent of photography. In fact, Herschel suggested to Talbot that he use the camera lucida to draw landscapes, something that Herschel himself continued throughout his life. It was Talbot’s inability to draw even with the help of optical devices that inspired him to invent photographic processes.

properties.name: Francis Towne
properties.biography: Towne was a drawing teacher and painter in Exeter with a devoted local following but little traction in the London market. His idiosyncratic watercolors from tours through Wales (1777), Italy (1780–81, with John “Warwick” Smith), and the Lake District (1786) offer fresh perspectives on the landscape, beyond the generally favored tradition established by Claude Lorrain.

properties.name: Victor Marie Hugo
properties.biography: Hugo’s international fame as a novelist, poet, and public intellectual far exceeded his reputation as a visual artist, but he was a prolific, experimental, and visionary draftsman for much of his adult life. Among his most intensely creative periods was his exile on Jersey and Guernsey (1853–70), when he responded in drawings to the natural setting and local encounters or let his imagination wander freely. Hugo presented small drawings to visitors as souvenirs but only rarely published reproductions with his writings.

properties.name: Berthe Morisot
properties.biography: Morisot took lessons in art from an early age and was registered as a copyist at the Louvre. Camille Corot introduced her to outdoor painting, which she practiced with watercolors. A regular contributor to the Salon beginning in 1864, Morisot exhibited at all but one of the Impressionist exhibitions between 1874 and 1886. She studied works by J. M. W. Turner and John Constable during a visit to England in 1875 and spent time in Italy in 1881–82. Married to Edouard Manet’s brother, Morisot was a fixture in the most advanced Parisian art circles.

properties.name: Gustave Doré
properties.biography: A highly prolific illustrator of literature who also excelled as a sculptor and painter, Doré had a lifelong interest in painting the landscape in watercolor and oil, nurtured by his travels to the Pyrenees, Alps, and Scottish Highlands. He exhibited at the Paris Salon from 1848 to 1882 and opened the Doré Gallery in London in 1868 with great success.

properties.name: Eugène Isabey
properties.biography: As the son of artist Jean-Baptiste Isabey, Eugène grew up in the Paris art scene and frequently received awards for contributions to the Salon once he began submitting. His trips to Britain (1821 and 1825, when 290 Artist Biographies he befriended Eugène Delacroix) and Algiers (1830) proved formative. He practiced large-scale history painting and pictured the landscapes of Normandy. Friendships with Louis-Eugène Boudin and Johan Barthold Jongkind connected him to the next eneration. g
